claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. ... private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking. | probe-01 (tsc 5.9.3): exit 0, no diagnostics
claim_checks.note: The handbook gives the type-check-only rule and runtime access for both modifiers, but grants the bracket-notation escape hatch and the 'soft private' label to `private` only. The `protected` bracket case rests on probe-01 alone. The probe is valid (a TS2445 error would make tsc exit non-zero) and passes, but it shows one compiler version (TypeScript 5.9.3), while the claim states it as a general rule with no version.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. ... Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The first sentence is supported. The second sentence attributes 'will degrade' to the handbook, but the handbook says 'could affect'. That raises 'could' to 'will', a MUST-level word, so the severity is CRITICAL_FAIL. The handbook's note also covers hard-privacy mechanisms in general (closures, WeakMaps, private fields), not only the downlevelled output.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields.
claim_checks.page_says: For this reason, structuredClone() does not clone private elements, and Object.freeze() and Object.seal() have no effect on private elements. | probe-02 stdout: false
claim_checks.note: The first two sentences are supported by MDN ('cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method'). The structuredClone clause says the opposite of MDN. The cited probe is valid: it checks `#x in` the clone, it could print true, and it prints false. So the probe also disproves the clause. The doc's own Probes section describes the same probe as showing that the copy 'has no # field'.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown ... This will return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise.
claim_checks.note: MDN's example error text reads 'Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it'.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.4 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: The first issue has been fixed in V8 v9.7 ... Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations.
claim_checks.note: The page gives v9.7, not 9.4, so the version is wrong. The doc's own front matter also says 'V8 ≥ 9.7'. The claim also drops a condition: V8 uses the new inline cache only 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough', and otherwise falls back to a runtime call.

claim_checks.claim: A `#` name cannot be a parameter property (context: injected collaborator row, form `private readonly x` constructor parameter).
claim_checks.page_says: That this is not possible is a bit surprising because it increases the friction of refactoring from a TypeScript-only concept to a native JavaScript feature
claim_checks.note: The issue text supports the statement. However, a Rank 6 source is cited in a role-3 section, where ranks 1–4 are allowed: KB-15 breach, logged as a separate violation. The handbook [^1] Parameter Properties passage lists only public, private, protected or readonly as parameter-property prefixes, so it could carry this row.

claim_checks.claim: In Node 24.22.1, `Object.getOwnPropertyNames()` never lists a `#` field
claim_checks.page_says: try { const names = Object.getOwnPropertyNames(...); if (names.length > 5) throw new Error('unexpected'); } catch {} console.log('not listed'); | stdout: not listed
claim_checks.note: The probe cannot fail. It swallows every error with an empty catch, prints 'not listed' whatever happens, and never checks whether the name list contains a private field: it only tests length > 5, which a two-field class can never exceed. It also cannot support 'never'.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied (context: object wrapped in a Proxy; `#` access does not go through the proxy).
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it (context: target ES2021 or lower; `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups).
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor (context: `--experimental-transform-types` runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning, re-tested 2026-11-03; the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0).
claim_checks.page_says: Removed --experimental-transform-types flag. (history row v26.0.0). Not found: any ExperimentalWarning for this flag on 24.x (searched 'transform', 'experimental', 'warning').
claim_checks.note: The removal in 26.0.0 is supported. The Node 24.22 ExperimentalWarning behaviour comes from a local re-test with no probe, yet it is attributed to [^4], which does not show it. The recommendation is the author's inference, not something the page says.

claim_checks.claim: Node only deletes types (context: type stripping stable, stability 2, since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores tsconfig.json and needs .ts extensions in relative imports).
claim_checks.page_says: v25.2.0, v24.12.0 | Type stripping is now stable. ... v24.3.0, v22.18.0 | Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning. ... Since Node.js is only removing inline types
claim_checks.note: The page also says 'Stability: 2 - Stable', 'Node.js ignores tsconfig.json files', and that file extensions are mandatory in import statements.

conflicts.topic: Whether structuredClone() copies private elements (How it works 4 says it copies them like public fields)
conflicts.loser: the doc's own wording; no cited source supports it

conflicts.topic: V8 version that moved class-field initialization to the inline cache (How it works 6 says 9.4)
conflicts.loser: the doc's own wording; no cited source supports it, and the front matter says 9.7

violations.evidence: C3: the claim says the handbook notes the checks 'will degrade performance'; [^1] says they 'could affect performance' (modal raised to MUST level).
C4: 'structuredClone() copies them like public fields'; [^2] says 'structuredClone() does not clone private elements', and the cited probe-02 prints false. Recorded under conflicts too; counted once.
C6: 'V8 9.4'; [^3] says the fix shipped in 'V8 v9.7' (wrong version). Recorded under conflicts too; counted once.
C8: probe-03 wraps its check in try { ... } catch {} and then runs console.log('not listed') unconditionally; it never tests whether a private name is listed, so it cannot fail (invalid_probe).
The 'Where each form fits' table (role 3, ranks 1–4 allowed) cites [^5], a GitHub issue (rank 6), for 'A # name cannot be a parameter property'.

C1: [^1] grants bracket-notation access during type checking and the 'soft private' label to `private` only; the `protected` part rests on probe-01 (TypeScript 5.9.3) alone but is written as a general rule with no version.
C11: the Node 24.22 ExperimentalWarning behaviour of --experimental-transform-types is not in [^4]; it rests on a local re-test with no probe.
[^6] (TC39 class fields proposal) is listed as backing 'How it works 2' but is never cited in the body.

It reports 10 verified claims; the body has 12 ✅-closed claims (14 marks). The Summary's and Takeaways' performance statements ('costs the same', 'measured cost is nil') rest on the Worked example's uncited, unmarked benchmark, whose construction times (166–172 ms vs 168–180 ms) do not show a nil cost.

No section does the role-2 (concept architecture) or role-5 (reference and invariants) job. A decision table ('Where each form fits') sits inside the mechanism section, and version reference values sit in Edge cases.

patch_instructions.action: Item 1: limit the bracket-notation clause and the 'soft private' label to `private`, per [^1] ('private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking'). State the protected case separately as an observation: 'In TypeScript 5.9.3, bracket access to a `protected` member also type-checks ✅[^probe-01]'.

Item 3: replace 'will degrade performance' with 'could affect performance', and attribute it to runtime hard-privacy mechanisms in general, per [^1] ('Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance').

Item 4: replace 'and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields' with '`structuredClone()` does not clone private elements, and `Object.freeze()`/`Object.seal()` have no effect on them', per [^2]. Keep probe-02 worded as 'In Node 24.22.1, a structuredClone() copy has no `#` field'.
Item 6: change 'V8 9.4' to 'V8 v9.7', and add the condition 'when V8 considers the initialization pattern predictable enough; otherwise it falls back to a runtime call', per [^3].

'Where each form fits' table, injected-collaborator row: replace ✅[^5] with [^1]'s Parameter Properties passage (parameter properties are 'created by prefixing a constructor argument with one of the visibility modifiers public, private, protected, or readonly'), rewording it to match. Or move the table to ## Trade-offs (role 6), where [^5] may stay, labelled as a rank-6 issue thread.

Rewrite probe-03 so it can fail: drop the try/catch and print the actual list, for example `console.log(JSON.stringify(Object.getOwnPropertyNames(new (class { #x = 1; y = 2 })())))` with expect stdout `["y"]`. Reword the claim as 'In Node 24.22.1, Object.getOwnPropertyNames() on an instance with `#x` and `y` returns ["y"]' (no 'never'). Until then, remove the ✅.
Cite [^6] in How it works item 2 (the proposal says 'It's impossible to access the private field from outside of the class'), or delete the [^6] entry.
--experimental-transform-types row: keep [^4] only for 'removed in Node 26.0.0'. Mark the Node 24.22 ExperimentalWarning statement ⚠️, or back it with a probe run on node:24.22.1.

Recount the ✅ and ⚠️ claims after the fixes (the body currently has 12 ✅-closed claims, not 10). Either cite or probe the Worked example benchmark, or soften the Summary's 'costs the same' and the Takeaways' 'measured cost is nil' to match the measured ranges.
